title: Perform primary meat inspection incisions of ostrich

lessons.title: Ostrich slaughter and preparing for inspection
lessons.html:
The ostrich industry

South Africa is the world's largest producer of ostrich products, with most farming in the Klein Karoo and the Western Cape. Ostrich meat is lean red meat and much of it is exported, so inspection must meet both the regulations under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and the requirements of importing countries. Ostriches are slaughtered at abattoirs registered for ostrich; their skins (leather) and feathers are valuable by-products.

How ostrich inspection differs from mammals

  • Birds do not have lymph nodes like cattle and sheep. Inspection therefore relies more on observation, palpation and incision of organs and muscle than on lymph node incisions.
  • Birds have air sacs, thin membranes connected to the lungs, which must be examined for inflammation (airsacculitis).
  • Ostriches have a proventriculus and a muscular gizzard, and often swallow stones and foreign objects.

Preparing the station

  • Good lighting at viscera and carcass inspection points.
  • A system that keeps the viscera, heart, liver and lungs matched to each carcass number.
  • Sterilizer, hand-wash basin, two sharp knives, steel and hook.
  • Detention rail, tags and condemned containers.
  • PPE suitable for the plant.

Planning

  1. Check ante-mortem findings, such as birds that are lame, thin, injured, or show breathing problems or diarrhoea.
  2. Note any official disease controls in force, for example for avian influenza, which is a controlled disease and has affected ostrich farms in the Western Cape. Follow the veterinarian's instructions for such birds.
  3. Confirm procedures for stopping the line and diverting carcasses.

lessons.title: Performing the inspection of ostrich
lessons.html:
Routine examination

Follow the sequence and incisions in which you were trained and which the regulations require. The main areas are:

Carcass

  • Observe the skinned carcass for bruising, haemorrhages, fractures (especially legs and pelvis), abscesses and injection-site lesions.
  • Assess condition: an emaciated ostrich has wasted thigh muscles and serous (watery, jelly-like) fat.
  • Check for contamination with feathers, faeces or ingesta.
  • Incise muscle where lesions are suspected; the large thigh muscles carry most of the valuable meat.

Respiratory system

  • Observe the air sacs: normal air sacs are thin and transparent. Thick, cloudy or yellow air sacs with cheesy material indicate airsacculitis.
  • Observe and palpate the lungs for consolidation, nodules and abscesses.

Heart and liver

  • Observe the heart sac and heart for pericarditis, haemorrhages and abnormal fluid.
  • Observe and palpate the liver; incise where lesions are seen. Look for abscesses, enlargement, discolouration and spots that may indicate infection.

Digestive tract and other organs

  • Observe the proventriculus and gizzard. Impaction with sand, stones, grass or foreign objects such as wire, nails and plastic is common, and may cause perforation and peritonitis.
  • Observe the intestines, spleen and kidneys for inflammation, enlargement and haemorrhage.

Technique and hygiene

  • Keep incisions neat to protect the value of the meat.
  • Sterilise after every bird and after cutting into a lesion.
  • Do not puncture the digestive tract.

lessons.title: Completing the ostrich inspection
lessons.html:
Findings and actions

FindingAction
No abnormalitiesCarcass continues for marking
Localised bruise or old fractureMark for trimming
Gizzard impaction without peritonitisCondemn affected organs; carcass continues if normal
Perforation with peritonitisDetain and refer; may lead to total condemnation
AirsacculitisDetain; judgement depends on extent and signs of generalisation
Emaciation with serous fatDetain and refer
Signs suggesting a controlled diseaseStop, detain and report immediately

Executing actions

  • Tag detained carcasses together with all their organs.
  • Ensure trimming is complete before marking.
  • Secure condemned material in marked, lockable containers.

Records and export requirements

Accurate records are especially important because much ostrich meat is exported. Record bird number, producer, findings, condemnations and detentions. Export markets may require traceability of each bird back to the farm and records of disease control measures.

Feedback

  • To producers: high rates of impaction or foreign bodies point to camp management problems, such as wire and rubbish in the camps. Bruising points to handling and transport problems.
  • To the line: contamination and dressing faults.

Key points

  • Birds lack typical lymph nodes, so ostrich inspection relies on observing, palpating and incising organs and muscle.
  • Examine the air sacs for airsacculitis.
  • Check the proventriculus and gizzard for impaction, foreign bodies and perforation.
  • Avian influenza is a controlled disease: suspected cases must be reported immediately.
  • Keep exact records for traceability and export.
